query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying equal-atomic NbMoTaW with a small concentration of interstitial boron (∼0.1 at%) will significantly improve its room-temperature ductility by segregating to grain boundaries and enhancing cohesion—thus promoting uniform plastic flow—while leaving its high-temperature strength (at 1600 °C) and irradiation resistance essentially unchanged.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast and homogenized equal-atomic NbMoTaW with an average grain size of ~20 µm, no B doping
generation.intervention: Addition of 0.1 at% boron during melting (stir-casting) followed by the same thermo-mechanical processing route as baseline
generation.conditions: (1) Quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature; (2) Compression tests at 1600 °C; (3) 1 MeV Kr²⁺ ion irradiation up to 10 dpa at 600 °C
generation.structural_mediator: B segregation at grain boundaries reducing intergranular fracture propensity
generation.mechanism: Interstitial B atoms migrate to and decorate grain boundaries, lowering grain-boundary energy and enhancing cohesion; this facilitates dislocation transmission across boundaries at RT, improving ductility. At 1600 °C B remains in solid solution (no gross precipitates), thus preserving creep and strength. Under irradiation B clusters act as defect sinks, maintaining baseline swelling and hardening behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Room-temperature total elongation increases from <1% to ~5–10%; 1600 °C yield strength remains within ±10% of the undoped baseline (~400–500 MPa); irradiation swelling and hardness changes remain within ±5% of baseline.
generation.baseline: Undoped NbMoTaW: room-temperature elongation <1%, 1600 °C yield ~450 MPa, negligible swelling under 10 dpa Kr irradiation
generation.boundary: B content between 0.05–0.2 at%; grain size 10–50 µm; no detectable B-rich second phases; irradiation temperature ≤600 °C
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of ductility gain and precise segregation behavior are uncertain; risk of boride formation if B exceeds ~0.2 at%

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloys—NbMoTaW and NbMoTaW+0.1 at% B—under identical melting and forging. Use atom-probe tomography/EBSD to map B distribution. Perform RT tensile tests, 1600 °C compression tests, and 1 MeV Kr²⁺ irradiation to 10 dpa at 600 °C on both.
measurements: Atom-probe elemental maps of B distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if the B-doped alloy shows <3% absolute increase in RT elongation or >10% drop in 1600 °C strength or >5% increase in irradiation swelling compared to baseline.
